tip: Prices use 'it makes': Πόσο κάνει; (póso káni = how much does it make?) is the everyday 'how much is it?'
Prices 'make' in Greek: κάνει (kani) in Ο καφές κάνει τρία ευρώ is literally 'the coffee makes three euros'. That's normal shop talk – κοστίζει (kostizi = costs) sounds more formal.

english: I want two kilos of tomatoes.
tip: No word for 'of' after amounts – the noun just follows: δύο κιλά ντομάτες (dío kilá domátes = two kilos tomatoes).

target: Το τυρί κάνει οχτώ ευρώ το κιλό.
english: The cheese costs eight euros a kilo.
tip: The article works as 'per': οχτώ ευρώ το κιλό (ochtó evró to kiló = eight euros the kilo) – no extra word needed.
'Three' agrees: τρία (tría) with neuter nouns like τρία παιδιά (tría pediá = three children), τρεις (tris) with masculine and feminine.
With several items the price verb goes plural: Πόσο κάνουν δύο καφέδες; (póso kánoun dío kafédes = how much are two coffees?)

english: I want half a kilo of olives.
tip: μισό (misó = half) agrees with its noun: μισό κιλό (misó kiló), but feminine μισή ώρα (misí óra = half an hour).
The ; ending Τι ώρα είναι; (Ti ora ine) is the Greek question mark – Greek asks with a semicolon, not ?. Its own pause mark is a raised dot (·) instead.
Even numbers carry gender: it's τρεις (treis) because the unspoken ώρες (ores = hours) is feminine. Counting euros, 'three' becomes τρία (tria).
'At' + clock time is στις (stis): στις εννιά (stis enniá = at nine). Hours count as a feminine plural, hence the plural 'at'.
στις δύο (stis dyo = at two) uses a plural 'the' because clock times count feminine ώρες (ores = hours). Only one o'clock goes singular: στη μία (sti mia).

english: I wake up at seven in the morning.
tip: Parts of the day need no 'in' – just the article: το πρωί (to proí = in the morning), το βράδυ (to vrádi = in the evening).

english: We have an appointment at one.
tip: One o'clock is the odd one out: στη μία (sti mía), not στις (stis) – one is a single hour, so the 'at' word goes singular too.
Half past is 'and half': δώδεκα και μισή (dódeka ke misí = twelve and half = 12:30).

target: Το λεωφορείο φεύγει σε δεκαπέντε λεπτά.
english: The bus leaves in fifteen minutes.
tip: σε (se) + a time span means 'in': σε δεκαπέντε λεπτά (se dekapénde leptá = in fifteen minutes).
Days are feminine – η Δευτέρα (i Deftéra = Monday), η Τρίτη (i Tríti = Tuesday) – except neuter το Σάββατο (to Sávato).

target: Την Τετάρτη δουλεύω από το σπίτι.
english: On Wednesday I work from home.
tip: No word for 'on' with days – the article alone does it: την Τετάρτη (tin Tetárti = on Wednesday).

english: On Saturday I go to the market.
tip: No word for 'on' with days: Το Σάββατο (To Savvato) is just 'the Saturday'. Every day works this way – only the article matches the day's gender: Την Τρίτη (Tin Triti = on Tuesday).
No 'I' needed – the -ω ending of πίνω (pino) already marks the speaker. Greek drops subject pronouns unless you're stressing who does it.
Greek questions keep statement word order – no 'do'. Εσύ τρως κρέας; (esi tros kreas) = 'you eat meat?', asked by tone alone. That ; at the end is the Greek question mark.
Negation is just δεν (den) before the verb: δεν τρώω (den troo) = 'I don't eat'. No helper word like English 'do'.
Hunger is a verb, not a feeling you 'are': Πεινάω πολύ (pináo polí = I hunger a lot) – no 'am' anywhere.
Thirst is a verb in Greek: διψάει (dipsai) means 'is thirsty' – the baby thirsts. Hunger works the same way: πεινάει (peinai).

target: Το τυρί εδώ είναι πολύ καλό.
english: The cheese here is very good.
tip: Talking about cheese in general still needs 'the': το τυρί (to tiri). Greek keeps the article where English drops it.
Ordering just names the item: Δύο καφέδες, παρακαλώ (dío kafédes parakaló). A single coffee changes shape: έναν καφέ (énan kafé), not ένας (énas).
'The bill' changes shape as an object: ο λογαριασμός (o logariasmos) becomes τον λογαριασμό (ton logariasmo). Articles and endings shift with the noun's role.

target: Ένα τσάι και έναν καφέ, παρακαλώ.
english: One tea and one coffee, please.
tip: 'One' matches its noun: ένα τσάι (ena tsai) but έναν καφέ (enan kafe) – masculine nouns as objects add -ν to the word for 'one'.

english: I go to the market in the morning.
tip: One word covers to, in, and at: σε (se). It fuses with 'the': σε + την becomes στην αγορά (stin agora) = to the market.

english: Are we going to the taverna tonight?
tip: Πάμε (pame) is both 'we go' and 'let's go / shall we?' – the same form makes the statement and the invitation.

target: Πας στη δουλειά με το λεωφορείο;
english: Do you go to work by bus?
tip: στην (stin) loses its ν before most consonants: στη δουλειά (sti douliá = to work). It keeps the ν before vowels and hard sounds like k, p, t.
